name: Aorta
summary: The largest artery in the body. It receives the entire left ventricular output and, through elastic recoil, converts pulsatile ejection into continuous peripheral flow.

anatomy.location: Begins at the aortic valve, ascends behind the sternum, arches posteriorly and to the left over the left main bronchus, descends through the posterior mediastinum, and passes through the diaphragm at the level of T12 to become the abdominal aorta.
anatomy.shape: Divided into the root (with the sinuses of Valsalva), the ascending aorta, the arch, and the descending thoracic and abdominal segments. Its wall is rich in elastic lamellae, giving it the compliance on which the Windkessel effect depends. Normal ascending aortic diameter in adults is roughly 2.5–3.5 cm.
relations: Ascending aorta lies within the pericardium, anterior to the right pulmonary artery and to the right of the pulmonary trunk
The arch gives the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries
The ligamentum arteriosum tethers the arch at the isthmus, just distal to the left subclavian — the classic site of traumatic transection and of coarctation
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks beneath the arch, which is why aneurysm can cause hoarseness
The descending thoracic aorta lies behind the left atrium and adjacent to the oesophagus
attachments: Aortic annulus and the crown-shaped attachment of the aortic valve cusps
Aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12
anatomy.bloodSupply: Vasa vasorum supplying the outer media and adventitia; the inner media is nourished by diffusion from the lumen.
anatomy.venousDrainage: Small veins accompanying the vasa vasorum.
anatomy.innervation: Sympathetic and vagal fibres; baroreceptors in the aortic arch are innervated by the vagus nerve and signal to the brainstem cardiovascular centres.
anatomy.function: Conducts blood to the systemic circulation and, critically, stores energy in its elastic wall during systole, releasing it in diastole to maintain forward flow and coronary perfusion.

physiology.function: Acts as an elastic reservoir (the Windkessel), damping the pulsatile output of the left ventricle so that capillary flow is near-continuous, and sustaining the diastolic pressure that drives coronary perfusion.

pressures.label: Systolic pressure
pressures.value: approximately 100–140 mmHg

pressures.label: Diastolic pressure
pressures.value: approximately 60–90 mmHg

pressures.label: Mean arterial pressure
pressures.value: roughly diastolic pressure plus one third of pulse pressure

pressures.label: Pulse pressure
pressures.value: approximately 40 mmHg; widens with age as the wall stiffens

physiology.electrical: Not electrically active. Aortic arch baroreceptors provide the afferent limb of the baroreflex through the vagus nerve.
hemodynamics: Windkessel function converts intermittent ejection into continuous peripheral flow
Arterial stiffening with age reduces compliance, raising systolic pressure and widening pulse pressure — the basis of isolated systolic hypertension
Pulse wave velocity increases with stiffness and is an independent cardiovascular risk marker
Laplace's law means wall tension rises with radius, so a dilating aneurysm becomes progressively more likely to rupture
The dicrotic notch on the aortic pressure trace marks aortic valve closure

pathology.name: Aortic aneurysm
pathology.note: Progressive dilatation with risk of rupture, related to hypertension, atherosclerosis, bicuspid valve aortopathy and connective tissue disease.

pathology.name: Aortic dissection
pathology.note: An intimal tear allowing blood into the media, creating a false lumen; a time-critical emergency.

pathology.name: Coarctation of the aorta
pathology.note: Narrowing near the isthmus producing upper limb hypertension and radiofemoral delay.

pathology.name: Atherosclerosis
pathology.note: Plaque throughout the aorta, a source of atheroembolism and a marker of systemic disease.

clinical.relevance: Aortic disease is often silent until catastrophic; recognising the presentation of dissection and knowing who to screen for aneurysm are core clinical competencies.
examination: Blood pressure difference between arms, and radiofemoral delay in coarctation
Tearing interscapular or chest pain with pulse deficits in dissection
Expansile pulsatile abdominal mass in abdominal aortic aneurysm
Early diastolic murmur if dissection involves the root and causes aortic regurgitation
imaging: CT angiography — the first-line investigation in suspected acute aortic syndrome
Transoesophageal echocardiography for the root and descending aorta
MR angiography for surveillance in younger patients and connective tissue disease
Abdominal ultrasound for aneurysm screening and follow-up
procedures: Open surgical repair and endovascular stent grafting (TEVAR and EVAR)
Valve-sparing root replacement and composite root replacement
Balloon angioplasty or stenting for coarctation
Aggressive blood pressure and heart rate control in type B dissection

keyPoints: Root, ascending, arch, descending thoracic and abdominal segments.
Arch branches: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian.
The isthmus, tethered by the ligamentum arteriosum, is the classic site of coarctation and traumatic transection.
Elastic recoil (Windkessel) maintains diastolic pressure and therefore coronary perfusion.
Aortic stiffening with age widens pulse pressure and causes isolated systolic hypertension.

name: Pulmonary Trunk
summary: Carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle towards the lungs — the only large artery in the adult carrying deoxygenated blood.

anatomy.location: Arises from the right ventricular infundibulum at the level of the third left costal cartilage, and runs superiorly and posteriorly for roughly 5 cm before bifurcating beneath the aortic arch.
anatomy.shape: A short, wide vessel about 5 cm long and 2.5–3 cm in diameter, with a thinner and more compliant wall than the aorta because it operates at far lower pressure. It lies within the pericardium along with the ascending aorta.
relations: Begins anterior and to the left of the ascending aorta, then spirals posteriorly
Enclosed with the ascending aorta in a common sleeve of pericardium — the basis of the transverse pericardial sinus behind them
Bifurcates beneath the aortic arch into right and left pulmonary arteries
The ligamentum arteriosum connects the bifurcation or left pulmonary artery to the undersurface of the arch
attachments: Pulmonary valve annulus at its origin
Ligamentum arteriosum at the bifurcation, the remnant of the ductus arteriosus
Pericardial reflection enclosing it with the aorta
anatomy.bloodSupply: Vasa vasorum from bronchial arteries and small branches of the coronary circulation.
anatomy.venousDrainage: Small veins accompanying the vasa vasorum.
anatomy.innervation: Cardiac and pulmonary plexuses; stretch receptors in the wall contribute to reflex responses.
anatomy.function: Conducts the entire right ventricular output into the pulmonary circulation while providing compliance that buffers right ventricular ejection.

physiology.function: Delivers the whole cardiac output to the lungs at roughly one fifth of systemic pressure, reflecting the very low resistance and high compliance of the pulmonary vascular bed.

pressures.label: Systolic pressure
pressures.value: approximately 15–30 mmHg

pressures.label: Diastolic pressure
pressures.value: approximately 8–15 mmHg

pressures.label: Mean pulmonary artery pressure
pressures.value: normally under about 20 mmHg

pressures.label: Pulmonary vascular resistance
pressures.value: roughly one tenth of systemic vascular resistance

physiology.electrical: Not electrically active, although myocardial sleeves extend a short distance into its wall and are an occasional arrhythmic source.
hemodynamics: The pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure, high-compliance, low-resistance system able to accommodate large increases in flow with only small pressure rises
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood from poorly ventilated regions, in contrast to the systemic circulation where hypoxia causes vasodilatation
Chronic pressure elevation causes vascular remodelling and right ventricular hypertrophy
Dilatation of the trunk can compress the left main coronary artery in severe pulmonary hypertension

pathology.name: Pulmonary hypertension
pathology.note: Mean pulmonary artery pressure above normal, from left heart disease, lung disease, thromboembolism or pulmonary arterial disease itself.

pathology.name: Pulmonary embolism
pathology.note: Saddle embolus at the bifurcation causes acute obstruction and right ventricular failure.

pathology.name: Patent ductus arteriosus
pathology.note: Persistence of the fetal ductus produces a continuous left-to-right shunt into the pulmonary trunk.

pathology.name: Pulmonary artery dilatation
pathology.note: Post-stenotic dilatation in pulmonary stenosis, or dilatation secondary to chronic pulmonary hypertension.

clinical.relevance: The pulmonary trunk is the entry point for pulmonary artery catheters and the target of catheter-directed therapy in massive pulmonary embolism; its size on imaging is a useful clue to pulmonary hypertension.
examination: Loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound
Left parasternal heave and a palpable P2
Continuous machinery murmur in patent ductus arteriosus
Raised JVP with a prominent a wave
imaging: CT pulmonary angiography for embolism and vessel calibre — a trunk wider than the adjacent ascending aorta suggests pulmonary hypertension
Echocardiography with tricuspid regurgitant velocity to estimate pulmonary artery systolic pressure
Ventilation–perfusion scanning for chronic thromboembolic disease
Right heart catheterisation — the definitive measurement
procedures: Right heart catheterisation and pulmonary artery catheter placement
Catheter-directed thrombolysis or embolectomy
Pulmonary endarterectomy for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
Device or surgical closure of a patent ductus arteriosus

keyPoints: The only large artery in the adult carrying deoxygenated blood.
Arises from the right ventricular infundibulum and bifurcates beneath the aortic arch.
Normal mean pressure is under about 20 mmHg — roughly one fifth of systemic.
Enclosed with the ascending aorta in a common pericardial sleeve.
The ligamentum arteriosum is the remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus.

name: Pulmonary Arteries
summary: The right and left branches of the pulmonary trunk, distributing deoxygenated blood through progressively smaller vessels to the alveolar capillary bed for gas exchange.

anatomy.location: The right pulmonary artery is longer and runs horizontally to the right behind the ascending aorta and superior vena cava; the shorter left pulmonary artery passes anterior to the descending aorta to reach the left hilum.
anatomy.shape: Thin-walled, highly compliant vessels that branch with the bronchial tree — lobar, then segmental, then arterioles, ending in the dense pulmonary capillary network surrounding the alveoli.
relations: Right pulmonary artery passes posterior to the ascending aorta and superior vena cava and anterior to the right main bronchus
Left pulmonary artery arches over the left main bronchus and is connected to the aortic arch by the ligamentum arteriosum
Within each hilum the artery lies in a constant relationship to the bronchus and pulmonary veins
Accompany the bronchial tree throughout the lung
attachments: Continuous proximally with the pulmonary trunk
Ligamentum arteriosum tethering the left pulmonary artery
anatomy.bloodSupply: Bronchial arteries supply the walls of the larger pulmonary arteries and the conducting airways — a dual blood supply that allows lung tissue to survive some embolic occlusion without infarction.
anatomy.venousDrainage: Bronchial veins, draining partly to the azygos system and partly to the pulmonary veins.
anatomy.innervation: Pulmonary plexus, with sympathetic and vagal contributions.
anatomy.function: Distribute deoxygenated blood evenly through the lung, matching perfusion to ventilation.

physiology.function: Deliver the entire cardiac output to the alveolar capillaries, where the very large surface area and thin blood–gas barrier allow rapid oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide release.

pressures.label: Mean pressure
pressures.value: normally under about 20 mmHg

pressures.label: Pulmonary capillary pressure
pressures.value: approximately 8–12 mmHg — low enough to prevent oedema

pressures.label: Transit time
pressures.value: roughly 0.75 s at rest; equilibration takes only about 0.25 s

pressures.label: Vascular recruitment
pressures.value: resistance falls as flow rises, through recruitment and distension

hemodynamics: Ventilation–perfusion matching depends on hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction redirecting flow away from poorly ventilated alveoli
Gravity produces regional differences in perfusion, classically described as West zones
Recruitment and distension allow flow to increase several-fold on exercise with minimal pressure rise
Because pulmonary capillary pressure is low, a rise in left atrial pressure is transmitted back and causes pulmonary oedema

pathology.name: Pulmonary embolism
pathology.note: Thrombus, usually from deep leg veins, lodging in the pulmonary arterial tree and causing dead-space ventilation and right ventricular strain.

pathology.name: Pulmonary arterial hypertension
pathology.note: Remodelling of small pulmonary arteries with intimal proliferation and plexiform lesions, raising resistance.

pathology.name: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
pathology.note: Organised, non-resolving thrombus causing fixed obstruction — potentially curable by endarterectomy.

pathology.name: Peripheral pulmonary stenosis
pathology.note: Branch narrowing seen in congenital syndromes such as Williams and Alagille.

clinical.relevance: Pulmonary embolism is among the most common causes of preventable in-hospital death, and pulmonary artery pressure is a key haemodynamic variable in heart failure and shock.
examination: Tachypnoea, tachycardia and pleuritic pain in acute embolism
Loud P2 and a right ventricular heave in pulmonary hypertension
Signs of deep vein thrombosis in the legs
Hypoxaemia with a clear chest in significant embolism
imaging: CT pulmonary angiography — the first-line test for suspected embolism
Ventilation–perfusion scanning, preferred for chronic thromboembolic disease and in pregnancy
Echocardiography for right ventricular strain and pressure estimation
Right heart catheterisation with pulmonary angiography
procedures: Systemic or catheter-directed thrombolysis
Percutaneous or surgical embolectomy
Pulmonary endarterectomy and balloon pulmonary angioplasty
Anticoagulation as the mainstay of treatment and prevention

keyPoints: The right pulmonary artery is longer and passes behind the ascending aorta and SVC.
Pulmonary arteries branch with the bronchial tree to reach the alveolar capillary bed.
The lung has a dual blood supply, so embolism does not always cause infarction.
Hypoxia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction — the opposite of the systemic response.
Low capillary pressure keeps alveoli dry; raised left atrial pressure causes pulmonary oedema.

name: Pulmonary Veins
summary: Four veins returning oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium — the only veins in the adult carrying oxygenated blood, and the source of most atrial fibrillation triggers.

anatomy.location: Two from each lung — superior and inferior — running from the hila to enter the posterior wall of the left atrium.
anatomy.shape: Thin-walled vessels without valves. Their proximal portions are invested by sleeves of left atrial myocardium extending 1–3 cm into the vein, which are electrically active. Variant anatomy is common, including a common left trunk and supernumerary right veins.
relations: Enter the posterior left atrial wall, which lies directly anterior to the oesophagus
At each hilum, the veins lie anterior and inferior to the bronchus and artery
The right veins pass behind the right atrium and superior vena cava
The left atrial appendage lies adjacent to the left superior pulmonary vein, separated by a ridge
attachments: Open into the posterior left atrium without valves
Myocardial sleeves continuous with left atrial muscle
anatomy.bloodSupply: Vasa vasorum; also receive some bronchial venous return, which accounts for a small physiological shunt.
anatomy.venousDrainage: They are the venous drainage of the pulmonary circulation.
anatomy.innervation: Ganglionated plexi cluster around the pulmonary vein–atrial junctions and modulate atrial electrophysiology.
anatomy.function: Return oxygenated blood to the left heart and provide a compliant reservoir between the pulmonary capillary bed and the left atrium.

physiology.function: Carry oxygenated blood at low pressure to the left atrium. Their pressure is effectively continuous with left atrial pressure because there are no intervening valves.

pressures.label: Pulmonary venous pressure
pressures.value: approximately 4–12 mmHg, equal to left atrial pressure

pressures.label: Oxygen saturation
pressures.value: approximately 95–100%

pressures.label: Threshold for pulmonary oedema
pressures.value: capillary pressure rising above roughly 20–25 mmHg

physiology.electrical: Myocardial sleeves have shortened refractory periods and abnormal automaticity, generating the ectopic beats that initiate most paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Their electrical isolation from the atrium is the cornerstone of ablation therapy.
hemodynamics: Pulmonary venous Doppler flow patterns are used to assess left atrial pressure and diastolic function
Because there are no valves, elevated left atrial pressure is transmitted directly back to the pulmonary capillaries
A small amount of bronchial venous drainage into the pulmonary veins creates a physiological right-to-left shunt

pathology.name: Atrial fibrillation
pathology.note: Pulmonary vein sleeves are the dominant source of triggering ectopy; isolating them is the basis of ablation.

pathology.name: Pulmonary vein stenosis
pathology.note: An uncommon but serious complication of ablation, causing dyspnoea, haemoptysis and localised congestion.

pathology.name: Anomalous pulmonary venous drainage
pathology.note: Partial or total drainage into the systemic venous system, producing a left-to-right shunt.

pathology.name: Pulmonary venous hypertension
pathology.note: Raised left atrial pressure from left heart disease transmitted backwards, causing pulmonary congestion.

clinical.relevance: Pulmonary vein anatomy is central to modern electrophysiology: every atrial fibrillation ablation begins with the question of how many veins there are and where their ostia lie.
examination: No specific signs; findings reflect the underlying condition
Irregularly irregular pulse in atrial fibrillation
Fixed splitting of the second heart sound with an associated atrial septal defect in partial anomalous drainage
imaging: Cardiac CT or MR venography to map ostia and variants before ablation
Transoesophageal echocardiography for vein flow and appendage assessment
Pulmonary venous Doppler on transthoracic echocardiography for diastolic function
procedures: Pulmonary vein isolation by radiofrequency, cryoballoon or pulsed-field ablation
Balloon angioplasty or stenting for post-ablation stenosis
Surgical rerouting for anomalous venous connections

keyPoints: Four veins — two from each lung — entering the posterior left atrium without valves.
The only veins in the adult carrying oxygenated blood.
Myocardial sleeves in their walls generate most atrial fibrillation triggers.
Pulmonary venous pressure equals left atrial pressure, so left heart disease causes pulmonary congestion.
Anatomical variants are common and must be mapped before ablation.

name: Superior Vena Cava
summary: Returns venous blood from the head, neck, upper limbs and thorax to the right atrium; the main route for central venous access and cardiac device leads.

anatomy.location: Formed behind the lower border of the right first costal cartilage by the union of the right and left brachiocephalic veins, and descending to enter the superior aspect of the right atrium at about the level of the third costal cartilage.
anatomy.shape: A short, wide, thin-walled and valveless vessel roughly 7 cm long. Its lower half lies within the pericardium.
relations: Anterior and to the right of the ascending aorta
The right phrenic nerve runs along its right side
The azygos vein arches forward over the right main bronchus to join its posterior aspect just above the pericardium
Surrounded by mediastinal lymph nodes, which is why bronchogenic carcinoma and lymphoma cause obstruction
attachments: Continuous above with the brachiocephalic veins
Opens into the right atrium at the cavoatrial junction, without a valve
anatomy.venousDrainage: It is itself a venous channel; the wall drains via small mediastinal veins.
anatomy.innervation: Autonomic fibres from the cardiac plexus; the adjacent right phrenic nerve is a key surgical landmark.
anatomy.function: Conducts roughly one third of systemic venous return to the right atrium.

physiology.function: Provides a low-pressure, valveless conduit whose pressure closely reflects right atrial pressure and which responds to changes in intrathoracic pressure.

pressures.label: Pressure
pressures.value: essentially equal to right atrial pressure, approximately 0–8 mmHg

pressures.label: Respiratory variation
pressures.value: flow increases and pressure falls with inspiration

pressures.label: Share of venous return
pressures.value: roughly one third of systemic venous return

physiology.electrical: Not electrically active, but myocardial sleeves at the cavoatrial junction, adjacent to the sinus node, can occasionally be an arrhythmic focus.
hemodynamics: Because it is valveless, right atrial pressure waves are transmitted directly into the jugular veins — the basis of the JVP
Negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration augments venous return through the SVC
Obstruction raises pressure in the head, neck and upper limbs and forces flow through collaterals such as the azygos system

pathology.name: Superior vena cava obstruction
pathology.note: Most often from malignant mediastinal disease, and increasingly from indwelling catheters and device leads; causes facial swelling and distended neck veins.

pathology.name: Persistent left superior vena cava
pathology.note: A common thoracic venous variant draining into a dilated coronary sinus; usually asymptomatic but important for device implantation.

pathology.name: Catheter-related thrombosis
pathology.note: Thrombus around central lines and pacing leads, which may propagate or embolise.

pathology.name: Sinus venosus defect
pathology.note: A defect near the SVC orifice, frequently with partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage.

clinical.relevance: The SVC is the highway for central lines, pacing leads and pulmonary artery catheters, and its obstruction is an oncological emergency that students should recognise on sight.
examination: Facial and upper limb swelling with plethora
Distended, non-pulsatile neck veins and dilated chest wall collateral veins
Pemberton's sign — facial congestion on raising the arms
Elevated JVP without a visible waveform in obstruction
imaging: Contrast CT of the chest to identify the level and cause of obstruction
Venography before device implantation where obstruction is suspected
Echocardiography with agitated saline to detect a persistent left SVC
Ultrasound for catheter-related thrombosis
procedures: Endovascular stenting for malignant obstruction
Central venous and pulmonary artery catheter insertion
Transvenous pacing and defibrillator lead placement
Lead extraction, in which the SVC is the site of greatest risk

keyPoints: Formed by the union of the two brachiocephalic veins; drains head, neck, upper limbs and thorax.
Valveless — so right atrial pressure is transmitted directly to the jugular veins.
Receives the azygos vein just before entering the pericardium.
Obstruction causes facial swelling, distended neck veins and collateral chest wall veins.
The main route for central venous access and cardiac device leads.

name: Inferior Vena Cava
summary: The largest vein in the body, returning blood from the abdomen, pelvis and lower limbs to the right atrium; its diameter and collapsibility are used to estimate right atrial pressure.

anatomy.location: Formed by the union of the common iliac veins at approximately L5, ascending to the right of the aorta, grooving the posterior liver, and piercing the central tendon of the diaphragm at T8 before entering the right atrium almost immediately.
anatomy.shape: A large, thin-walled, valveless vessel. Its right atrial orifice is guarded by the rudimentary Eustachian valve, which in fetal life directed oxygenated blood towards the foramen ovale.
relations: Lies to the right of the abdominal aorta throughout its abdominal course
Grooves the bare area of the liver and receives the hepatic veins just below the diaphragm
Passes through the caval opening of the diaphragm at T8
Retroperitoneal, with the right renal artery, right adrenal gland and duodenum among its anterior and posterior relations
attachments: Formed by the confluence of the common iliac veins
Receives renal, hepatic, gonadal, lumbar and adrenal tributaries
Opens into the inferior aspect of the right atrium, guarded by the Eustachian valve
anatomy.bloodSupply: Vasa vasorum from adjacent lumbar and renal vessels.
anatomy.venousDrainage: It is the principal venous channel of the lower body.
anatomy.function: Returns roughly two thirds of systemic venous return to the right atrium.

physiology.function: Carries the largest share of venous return and serves, with the rest of the venous system, as the body's principal blood reservoir.

pressures.label: Pressure
pressures.value: close to right atrial pressure, approximately 0–8 mmHg

pressures.label: Normal diameter
pressures.value: approximately 1.5–2.1 cm at end-expiration

pressures.label: Inspiratory collapse
pressures.value: greater than 50% collapse suggests a normal right atrial pressure

pressures.label: Share of venous return
pressures.value: roughly two thirds

physiology.electrical: Not electrically active. The cavotricuspid isthmus between the IVC orifice and the tricuspid annulus is the critical zone in typical atrial flutter.
hemodynamics: Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure and raises intra-abdominal pressure, both of which augment IVC flow
IVC diameter and collapsibility are used at the bedside to estimate right atrial pressure and assess volume status
Compression by a gravid uterus in the supine position reduces venous return — the basis of left lateral tilt in pregnancy
Raised right atrial pressure causes hepatic venous congestion, hepatomegaly and ascites

pathology.name: Deep vein thrombosis and IVC thrombosis
pathology.note: Thrombus propagating from iliofemoral veins, with risk of pulmonary embolism.

pathology.name: IVC plethora
pathology.note: A dilated, non-collapsing IVC indicating raised right atrial pressure, as in right heart failure or tamponade.

pathology.name: Budd–Chiari syndrome
pathology.note: Hepatic venous outflow obstruction, sometimes involving the IVC, causing congestive hepatopathy.

pathology.name: Tumour extension
pathology.note: Renal cell carcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma can extend into and along the IVC lumen.

clinical.relevance: Bedside ultrasound of the IVC has become a routine part of assessing volume status in acute care, and the cavotricuspid isthmus adjacent to its orifice is the standard ablation target for typical atrial flutter.
conditions: Right heart failure with venous congestion
examination: Raised jugular venous pressure and hepatojugular reflux
Tender, pulsatile hepatomegaly, ascites and peripheral oedema
Dilated abdominal wall veins in chronic obstruction
Kussmaul's sign — a paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration — in constrictive physiology
imaging: Point-of-care ultrasound for IVC diameter and collapsibility
CT or MR venography for thrombosis and tumour extension
Echocardiography from the subcostal window
Fluoroscopy during flutter ablation and filter placement
procedures: Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation for typical atrial flutter
IVC filter placement in selected patients who cannot be anticoagulated
Femoral venous access for right heart catheterisation and electrophysiology
Surgical caval resection or reconstruction in tumour extension

keyPoints: The largest vein in the body, carrying roughly two thirds of systemic venous return.
Passes through the diaphragm at T8 and enters the right atrium almost immediately.
Its orifice bears the rudimentary Eustachian valve, important in fetal circulation.
IVC diameter and collapsibility estimate right atrial pressure on bedside ultrasound.
The cavotricuspid isthmus next to its orifice is the ablation target in typical atrial flutter.
